topics: Life After Death: Christianity and Islam

data.title: Resurrection, Akhirah, and Judgement
data.sourcePassage: Both Christianity and Islam teach that death is not the end and that a person will face judgement by God. Christianity places resurrection at the heart of its hope: Jesus rose from the dead, and believers trust they will also be raised in transformed bodily form. After death comes judgement — God assesses each person's life. Heaven is eternal life in God's presence for the saved; hell is separation from God. Catholic teaching includes purgatory, a state of purification before heaven. Islam teaches Akhirah — the term for life after death and one of the Six Articles of Faith. When a person dies, the soul enters Barzakh, a state of waiting until Yawm al-Qiyama (the Day of Judgement). On that day, all people are raised and their deeds are weighed. Those whose good deeds outweigh bad enter Jannah (paradise), described in the Qur'an as a beautiful garden of peace. Those who rejected Allah or acted wrongly face Jahannam (hell). Belief in Akhirah shapes Muslim behaviour: all actions are recorded and will be judged, motivating prayer, Zakah, and ethical conduct in daily life.

topics: Life After Death: Hinduism and Buddhism

data.title: Samsara, Reincarnation, and Rebirth
data.sourcePassage: Hinduism and Buddhism both teach that there is a cycle of birth, death, and rebirth called samsara, but they understand it differently. Hinduism teaches that each person has an eternal, permanent soul called the atman, which does not die when the body dies. Instead, shaped by karma (the moral consequences of actions), the atman passes into a new body — this is reincarnation. The ultimate goal is moksha: liberation from samsara, when the atman merges with or rests in Brahman (ultimate reality). Buddhist teaching is distinctly different. Buddhism holds anatta — the teaching that there is no permanent self or fixed soul. What continues through rebirth is a stream of consciousness, not a fixed entity. Think of a candle lighting another candle: there is continuity but not the same flame. Karma still shapes this process — actions motivated by craving and delusion generate further rebirth; wisdom and compassion move towards liberation. The Buddhist ultimate goal is nirvana — the extinguishing of craving and the ending of the cycle. Nirvana is not a paradise like heaven but liberation: the ending of all that drives suffering and rebirth.

topics: Life After Death: Sikhism, Judaism, Humanism

data.title: Sikhism, Judaism, and the Humanist View
data.sourcePassage: Sikhism teaches a cycle of rebirth similar in some ways to Hindu belief, but with a distinctly personal dimension. The soul (jiv atma) passes through many lives, shaped by karma. The ultimate goal is mukti — liberation and union with Waheguru (God). Crucially, Sikhism teaches that mukti is achieved through God's grace (nadar) and devotion, not solely through one's own merit. Sikh funerals involve cremation, with continuous readings from the Guru Granth Sahib over several days. Jewish beliefs about the afterlife are more varied than in Christianity or Islam. The Torah focuses more on this-world ethics and community than on afterlife details. Some Jews believe in Olam Ha-Ba (the World to Come) and resurrection; others emphasise this-world justice (tikkun olam) and legacy. Humanists do not believe in any personal survival after death. When the brain stops, consciousness ends. But this does not make life meaningless — quite the opposite. Because this life is all there is, it is precious. Humanists believe people live on through legacy: in the memories of those who knew them, in the lives they influenced, and in the love they gave.
